Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Senator [[Michael Bennet]] was re-elected to a third term, defeating the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] candidate, businessman Joe O'Dea. Originally appointed to the seat in 2009,{{Cite web |last=Alexander Burns |title=Bennet to replace Salazar in Senate |url=https://www.politico.com/story/2009/01/bennet-to-replace-salazar-in-senate-017001 |access-date=2022-09-16 |website=POLITICO |date=January 2, 2009 |language=en}} Bennet won full terms in [[2010 United States Senate election in Colorado|2010]] and [[2016 United States Senate election in Colorado|2016]].{{Cite web |title=Colorado - Election Results 2010 - The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/elections/2010/results/colorado.html |access-date=2022-09-16 |website=www.nytimes.com}}{{Cite web |url=https://results.enr.clarityelections.com/CO/63746/184388/Web01/en/summary.html |title=Official Certified Results November 8, 2016 General Election |access-date=2022-09-16 |website=results.enr.clarityelections.com}} Bennet won by nearly 15 points, significantly outperforming his polling. His margin was the highest for a Democrat in a Senate election in Colorado since [[1974 United States Senate election in Colorado|1974]]. This was the first time in Bennet's Senate career that he received a majority of the vote. ==Democratic primary == ===Candidates=== Bennet was appointed to the U.S. Senate in January 2009 by [[Governor of Colorado|Governor]] [[Bill Ritter]] following the resignation of the incumbent Senator, [[Ken Salazar]], who become the [[United States Secretary of the Interior|Secretary of the Interior]] under President [[Barack Obama]]. Bennet was then narrowly elected in [[2010 United States Senate election in Colorado|2010]] for his first full term, defeating Representative [[Ken Buck]] with 48.08% of the vote. In the [[2016 United States Senate election in Colorado|2016 election]], he was re-elected to a second term with 49.97% of the vote, defeating [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[El Paso County, Colorado|El Paso County]] [[County Board of Commissioners|Commissioner]] Darryl Glenn. Due to some of his centrist positions, such as his opposition to [[Medicare for All]] and his support for [[hydraulic fracturing|fracking]], Bennet faced a potential challenge from the left, particularly from [[Joe Salazar]], a former state representative. Salazar ultimately opted to run for the [[Colorado Senate|Colorado State Senate]], and thus Bennet was easily renominated at the Democratic convention.{{Cite web | candidates declared their intention to seek the Republican nomination. However, instead of gathering the required number of signatures to be placed on the primary ballot, Bremer and most of the other candidates sought to earn the nomination by winning the required 30% of the delegate vote at the Colorado GOP convention in April 2022. As a result of the crowded field of candidates, delegate support was divided, with only State Representative Ron Hanks crossing the 30% threshold. Debora Flora, a radio show host, missed the ballot by a single percentage point, receiving 29% of the vote.{{cite web | url=https://coloradosun.com/2022/04/09/colorado-senate-race-republican-primary/ | title=Ron Hanks, who questions 2020 election results, beats 5 other candidates to make Colorado's Republican U.S. Senate primary ballot | date=April 9, 2022 }} With the other candidates eliminated, State Representative [[Ron Hanks]] and construction CEO Joe O'Dea were the only two candidates on the primary ballot. The contrast between the two Republicans was stark. Hanks supported a complete ban on abortion and echoed former president [[Donald Trump]]'s false assertions of widespread voter fraud in the [[2020 United States presidential election|2020 presidential election]], while the more moderate O'Dea expressed support for [[LGBT|LGBTQ]] rights, some abortion rights, and rejected Trump's false claims of widespread voter fraud.{{Cite web |date=2022-06-29 |title=Republican Joe O'Dea, who supports some abortion rights, wins Colorado Senate primary |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2022-election/republican-joe-odea-supports-abortion-rights-wins-colorado-senate-prim-rcna35573 |access-date=2024-08-30 |website=NBC News |language=en}}{{Cite news |last=Qiu |first=Linda |date=2023-08-17 |title=Fact-Checking the Breadth of Trump’s Election Lies |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/08/17/us/politics/trump-election-lies-fact-check.html |access-date=2026-10-16 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} Though O'Dea was initially considered the frontrunner as a result of his fundraising advantage, Hanks was buoyed by an attempt by Democrats to influence the primary. Democratic Colorado, an entity formed in June 2022, received roughly $4 million from the Senate Majority Fund, a PAC associated with Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer. They ran ads characterizing Hanks as "too conservative", in order to elevate Hanks over O'Dea, who was perceived as a stronger general election candidate.{{cite web | url=https://www.9news.com/article/news/local/next/ron-hanks-colorado-gop-primary-spending-democrats/73-371dc47a-3372-415c-a49e-4f163a3c767b | title=Filing reveals Schumer-aligned PAC funded ads that boosted Ron Hanks in Colorado's GOP primary | date=July 23, 2022 }} This attempt to interfere in the GOP primary was denounced by numerous former Colorado Democratic officials, including former governor [[Roy Romer]], and former senators [[Mark Udall]], [[Tim Wirth]], and [[Gary Hart]], who previously mounted unsuccessful attempts to win the Democratic nomination for president in [[1984 Democratic Party presidential primaries|1984]] and [[1988 Democratic Party presidential primaries|1988]].{{cite web | url=https://www.coloradopolitics.com/denver-gazette/democratic-leaders-call-party-mates-tactics-to-boost-ron-hanks-others-during-primary-unethical/article_579e3c8c-11dc-11ed-a8cd-0312513ba3d4.html | title=Democratic leaders call party mates' tactics to boost Ron Hanks, others during primary 'unethical' | date=August 2022 }} Despite the support from Democrats and his lobbying for the endorsement of [[Donald Trump]], Hanks was defeated by O'Dea by a 9% margin. Prevailing in [[2010 United States Senate election in Colorado|2010]], a year where Colorado was considered a swing state and Democrats performed very poorly, Bennet had a generally strong electoral history. He also outperformed [[Hillary Clinton]] on the same ballot in [[2016 United States Senate election in Colorado|2016]]. Ahead of 2022, Bennet was generally favored to win, though polling showed him as potentially vulnerable, largely due to the state of the economy and President Biden's [[2022 opinion polling on the Joe Biden administration#Job approval ratings|low approval ratings]].{{Cite web |last1=Paul |first1=Jesse |last2=Fish |first2=Sandra |last3=Nelson |first3=Delaney |date=2022-11-09 |title=Michael Bennet elected to his third U.S. Senate term as Colorado voters reject Republican Joe O'Dea |url=http://coloradosun.com/2022/11/08/michael-bennet-joe-odea-us-senate-results/ |access-date=2023-08-09 |website=[[The Colorado Sun]] |language=en-US}} Colorado had not elected a Republican to the U.S. Senate since [[Cory Gardner]] in [[2014 United States Senate election in Colorado|2014]], another very strong year for Republicans nationwide and while Colorado was still considered a swing state, even then Gardner only won narrowly. Bennet ultimately won reelection by a comfortable 14.6 point margin, outperforming Biden's victory two years prior and his own polling averages. Bennet also flipped three counties he had lost in his 2016 re-election bid, flipping [[Grand County, Colorado|Grand County]] by a narrow 1.1% and [[Chaffee County, Colorado|Chaffee County]], and [[Garfield County, Colorado|Garfield County]] by wide margins.
